glance: 270 km to Khagrachhari by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
alutila-cave.desc: Alutila is a hill just outside Khagrachhari town, and the cave runs right through it for a few hundred feet. Inside it is completely dark, damp and cool, with a stream trickling along the rocky floor, so visitors carry a torch or a traditional burning stick. Emerging at the far end into daylight is the moment people remember. The hilltop above also has a viewpoint over the town and surrounding ridges.
blocks: How to get there
About 15–20 minutes by CNG or jeep from Khagrachhari town on the Chattogram road.
Good to know
Bring a strong torch and shoes that can get wet. Avoid if you are uncomfortable in tight dark spaces. Foreigners need prior permission for the Chittagong Hill Tracts; check current advisories.

glance: Around 70–120 BDT per kg in local bazars in season
Khagrachhari town bazar and orchard areas in Panchhari and Guimara, June–July
khagrachhari-amrapali-mango.desc: In recent years Khagrachhari's hills have filled with mango orchards, and the district now grows tens of thousands of tonnes a year, mostly Amrapali. The fruit is small, deep orange inside and very sweet, and it ripens in June–July. It sells across the country, but in season you can buy it cheaply in local bazars.

garia-dance.desc: Garia is a traditional Tripura ritual and dance associated with the god Garia, performed in the days around the new year. Groups of dancers move from house to house with drums and flutes, and households offer them food and drink in return for blessings. Khagrachhari, with its large Tripura population, is one of the best places to see it.
blocks: Good to know
Ask before filming, and remember these are religious as well as festive occasions.

khagrachhari-horticulture-park.desc: The Zila Parishad Horticulture Park sits on the hills at the Zero Mile end of Khagrachhari town. Its best-known feature is a hanging bridge strung across a small lake between two hillocks, and a watchtower gives views over the town and the surrounding ridges. Families come for the gardens and the kids' zone, and a zipline and giant swing were added more recently. It is an easy stop on the way to or from Alutila.
blocks: How to get there
CNG or auto from Khagrachhari town (Shapla Chattar) to Zero Mile; a few minutes' ride.
Good to know
Go late afternoon for the view from the watchtower. The hanging bridge can get crowded on holidays.

glance: 270 km to Khagrachhari by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
debota-pukur.desc: Known in the Tripura language as Matai Pukhiri, 'lake of the gods', this small lake sits near the top of a hill in Nunchhari, reached by a long flight of steps. For the Tripura community it is holy, and pilgrims climb here to pray and make offerings, especially at festival times. The water is still and green, the setting quiet, and the views on the way up are worth the climb.
blocks: How to get there
Hire a CNG or jeep from Khagrachhari town to the foot of the hill (around 30–45 minutes), then climb.
Good to know
Respect the site's sanctity: no swimming, no litter, and remove shoes where asked.

glance: Khagrachhari town bazar and roadside stalls toward Dighinala and Matiranga
khagrachhari-malta.desc: Over recent years many hill farmers in Khagrachhari have planted malta, a sweet orange that stays green even when ripe. The fruit is juicy and mildly sweet, and roadside sellers and bazars fill with it in the harvest season. Buying directly from growers supports hill households.

ramgarh-lake.desc: Ramgarh is one of the oldest towns of the Hill Tracts, on the Feni river opposite Sabroom in Tripura. In the town a lake surrounded by low green hills has been made into a park with a hanging footbridge and walking paths. It is a calm place for an hour's stop, and nearby are old tea gardens and the BGB memorial. Few travellers bound for Sajek or Alutila come this way, so it rarely feels crowded.
blocks: How to get there
Ramgarh is on the Chattogram–Khagrachhari road; from Khagrachhari town take a bus or CNG toward Ramgarh (about 1.5 hours) and a rickshaw to the lake.
Good to know
This is a border town; carry ID and do not go near the river border at night.

richhang-waterfall.desc: Richhang lies a short distance from Alutila, down a steep path into a stream valley. The water first drops off a ledge and then flows over a broad, gently tilted rock face, which visitors slide down in the rainy season. The surrounding hills are planted with jhum crops and fruit gardens.
blocks: How to get there
From the Alutila area take a jeep or motorbike down the side road, then walk down steps to the falls.
Good to know
The rock is slippery; slide only where locals do and never after a heavy downpour. The climb back up is tiring.

glance: Indigenous textile shops in Khagrachhari town
rignai-risa-weaving.desc: Tripura women traditionally wear the rignai, a wrap skirt, and the risa, a breast cloth, both woven at home on small back-strap looms. Patterns are bold and geometric, in reds, blacks and other strong colours, and each design has a name. You can find handwoven pieces, along with Chakma and Marma textiles, in shops in Khagrachhari town.

sidol-hill-cuisine.desc: Sidol is made by fermenting small dried fish into a firm, strong-smelling paste, and it forms the base of many Chakma, Marma and Tripura curries and bhortas. Mashed with chillies, or cooked with bamboo shoot, wild greens or jackfruit, it gives a deep savoury taste. Hill restaurants in Khagrachhari serve set meals that include these dishes alongside jhum rice.

glance: 270 km to Khagrachhari by road, 7–9 hours by bus or car
hazachora-waterfall.desc: Hazachora drops down a mossy rock wall into a shallow pool in a narrow valley. The walk in takes only a short while through village gardens and bamboo, which makes it an easy add-on to the Sajek journey. Few travellers stop, so it is often peaceful.
blocks: How to get there
On the Khagrachhari–Dighinala–Sajek road; ask your jeep driver to stop at the turn-off and walk in.
Good to know
Best after rain, when the flow is strong. Keep to timings if you are joining the Sajek convoy.

glance: A full hill meal with rice, one curry and vegetables runs about 120–250 BDT

khagrachhari-hebang.desc: Hebang is a Chakma way of cooking: meat, fish or eggs are packed with spices and herbs into a green bamboo tube, or wrapped in banana leaf, and set on the fire. It uses very little oil, and the bamboo gives the food a smoky, grassy smell. In Khagrachhari restaurants it is poured straight from the tube into a bowl at the table; egg hebang (bada hebang) is a common choice.
